parole.significato: rag (low quality article of clothing)
parole.testo: Possibly sound-symbolic (per SSA) + -le, or alternatively possibly from North Germanic (compare Old Norse fetill).

parole.significato: a log or pole used as a ramp for hoisting logs, moving boats, etc.
parole.testo: Possibly from North Germanic (compare Old Norse hjól).

parole.significato: St. John's wort (plant of the genus Hypericum)
parole.testo: Unknown; if of the same origin as dialectal kuisma (“abscess, swelling”) (which is possible if the plant's name is in reference to its uses in folk medicine), then possibly from North Germanic (compare Norwegian Nynorsk kusme (“mumps”)).

parole.significato: Saturday (day of the week; the sixth day of the week in Finland and in the ISO 8601 standard)
parole.testo: From earlier *laugantaki (compare dialectal lauvantaki), borrowed from North Germanic (compare Old Norse laugardagr). parole.significato: long-handled hand net/scoop net/dip net
parole.testo: Variant of liippi, lippi, borrowed from North Germanic (compare Norwegian glip, Danish glib), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *glīpaną.

parole.significato: synonym of länkipatja (“horse collar cushion”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from North Germanic (compare Old Norse malr).

parole.significato: roe pouch
parole.testo: Borrowed from North Germanic. Cognates include Norwegian Nynorsk mauk, Icelandic mauk.

parole.significato: A being created to bring milk or butter to its creator.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from North Germanic, from the same origin as Swedish bära (“to carry, bear”).

parole.significato: poor, poor thing (one to be pitied)
parole.testo: Possibly derived from polkea; alternatively from North Germanic (compare Old Norse bǫl (“misfortune”)).

parole.significato: harlot, whore, (female) prostitute
parole.testo: Borrowed from a North Germanic language, compare Old Norse portkona (“harlot”) and Old English portcwene.

parole.significato: to languish (to lose strength and become weak)
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from North Germanic (compare Old Norse þrjóta). Cognate with Karelian riutuo.

parole.significato: a place to temporarily store game or fish
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from North Germanic (compare Old Norse sár (“large cask”)). Related to Karelian saiho.

parole.significato: camomile (plant of the genus Anthemis)
parole.testo: saura + -mo, probably from dialectal saura (“calla”), possibly of North Germanic origin (compare dialectal Norwegian Nynorsk saur (“bulrush”))

parole.significato: the forwardmost or aftmost rib on a boat
parole.testo: Probably a blend of two dialectal words; former from North Germanic (compare Old Norse sess; akin to Northern Sami siessi) and the latter (piestin) from Swedish fäst + -in.

parole.significato: oval, elliptical
parole.testo: soi- + -kea; possibly from the same root as sojottaa. Alternatively, possibly of North Germanic origin (compare Old Norse sveigr). Related to Karelian soikie.

parole.significato: Sunday (day of the week; the seventh and last day of the week in Finland and in the ISO 8601 standard)
parole.testo: Borrowed from North Germanic (compare Old Norse sunnudagr, sunundægi, Swedish söndag), or directly from Old Saxon sunnundag; ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag.

parole.significato: tight (firmly held, pulled or pushed together)
parole.testo: Possibly a borrowing from North Germanic, perhaps Old Swedish thiokker, thiukker (“thick, fat”), but this is semantically dubious.

parole.significato: Thursday (day of the week; the fourth day of the week in Finland and in the ISO 8601 standard)
parole.testo: Borrowed from North Germanic, probably Old Swedish þōrsdagher; ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”).

parole.significato: rowlock
parole.testo: Borrowed from North Germanic (compare Swedish tull, Proto-Germanic *þullaz, Proto-Germanic *þullō).

parole.significato: snow and rime that accumulates on tree branches and any solid structures in certain climatic conditions
parole.testo: Borrowed from a North Germanic language, compare Old Norse þykkr (“thick, bulky”), from Proto-Germanic *þekuz. Karelian tykky has the same origin. parole.significato: to try, attempt, endeavour/endeavor
parole.testo: According to Bentlin (2019), borrowed from North Germanic (compare Old Norse yrkja (“to work”)) and derived with + -ttää (< *ürki-ttä- ~ *ürk(ä)-ittä-); alternatively derived from yrki- (“moment, while”) (dialectal) + -ittää (compare dialectal Ingrian yrtyä (“to begin”), Estonian ürgama (“to begin”)
